Description

In 2015, someone created this puzzle to demonstrate the enormous size of the Bitcoin private-key space—or perhaps simply for fun. The creator selected one private key from each progressively larger range and sent an increasing reward to the corresponding Bitcoin address:

20 ≤ private key < 21 — 0.001 BTC
21 ≤ private key < 22 — 0.002 BTC
22 ≤ private key < 23 — 0.003 BTC
...
2255 ≤ private key < 2256 — 0.256 BTC
(32.896 BTC in total)

The creator provided the original puzzle description:

The private keys for Puzzles #1—70, as well as #75, #80, #85, #90, #95, #100, #105, #110, #115, #120, #125, #130, and #135, have already been found.

History

2015-01-15
A transaction distributed funds across 256 different Bitcoin addresses.
2017-07-11
Funds from addresses #161—256 were moved (tx) to the same number of addresses in the lower range, increasing their rewards. This was likely because P2PKH addresses use a 160-bit HASH160: above Puzzle #160, expanding the private-key range no longer provides a corresponding increase in security because different private keys can produce public keys with the same 160-bit hash.
2019-06-01
The puzzle creator created a transaction spending 1,000 satoshis from each of the addresses #65, #70, #75, #80, #85, #90, #95, #100, #105, #110, #115, #120, #125, #130, #135, #140, #145, #150, #155, and #160. This exposed their public keys on-chain, probably with the aim of comparing the difficulty of finding private keys for addresses with exposed public keys against those without.
2023-04-16
Somebody (maybe the owner) once again increased the rewards for the unsolved puzzles tenfold in this transaction. The resulting rewards ranged from 6.6 BTC for Puzzle #66 and 6.7 BTC for Puzzle #67 to 16 BTC for Puzzle #160.
2024-09-12
Puzzle #66 (6.6 BTC) was solved by 1Jvv4y (tx1). However, the original spending transaction was replaced by another transaction that sent 5.94 BTC to bc1qpk (tx2). Another address, 15XVN6, ultimately claimed the remaining 0.66 BTC (tx3).
2025-02-21
Puzzle #67 (6.7 BTC) was solved by bc1qfk. To avoid interception like that seen with Puzzle #66, the transaction was mined directly without first being broadcast to the public mempool.
2025-04-06
Puzzle #68 (6.8 BTC) was solved by bc1qfw. As with Puzzle #67, the transaction was mined directly without first being broadcast to the public mempool, avoiding the risk of interception.
2025-04-30
Puzzle #69 (6.9 BTC) was solved by bc1qlp less than one month after Puzzle #68, likely because its private key was near the beginning of the search range (0.72%). However, the original transaction (tx1) was publicly broadcast, leading to it being replaced multiple times (tx2, tx3). Ultimately, 15g7XH stole the prize (tx4).
2026-07-28

Puzzle #135 (13.5 BTC) was solved by RetiredCoder:

Solution

To solve the puzzle, you must iterate over the specified private keyspace and check the balance of each private key. The narrower the keyspace, the greater the chance of finding the private key. Currently, it is better to focus on solving puzzle #71 (due to its narrower keyspace) or #140 (utilizing the Baby-step giant-step or Pollard's kangaroo algorithm because of the exposed public key).

To automate this process, you can use the following methods and tools:

  • Use our Bitcoin Puzzle Solver
  • Browse private keys directory of the puzzle #71 (not highly effective)
  • Generate random keys within the keyspace of puzzle #71 (not highly effective)
  • Use KeyHunt for CPU search (example)

    71-bit puzzle search:

    ./keyhunt -m rmd160 -f 71.rmd -b 71 -l compress -R

    Contents of the input file 71.rmd:

    f6f5431d25bbf7b12e8add9af5e3475c44a0a5b8

    140-bit puzzle (BSGS) search:

    ./keyhunt -m bsgs -f 140.txt -b 140 -R

    Contents of the input file 140.txt:

    031f6a332d3c5c4f2de2378c012f429cd109ba07d69690c6c701b6bb87860d6640
  • Use RCKangaroo for GPU search (example)

    140-bit puzzle search:

    RCKangaroo.exe -dp 16 -range 139 -start 80000000000000000000000000000000000 -pubkey 031f6a332d3c5c4f2de2378c012f429cd109ba07d69690c6c701b6bb87860d6640
  • Use Kangaroo for GPU search puzzles with exposed public key (limited to a 125-bit interval search) (example)

    125-bit puzzle search:

    ./Kangaroo -gpu 125.txt

    Contents of the input file 125.txt:

    10000000000000000000000000000000
1fffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff
0233709eb11e0d4439a729f21c2c443dedb727528229713f0065721ba8fa46f00e
  • Use BitCrack for GPU search (example)

    71-bit puzzle search:

    xxBitCrack.exe --keyspace 400000000000000000:7fffffffffffffffff -c 1PWo3JeB9jrGwfHDNpdGK54CRas7fsVzXU
  • Join one of the collective solving pools
